title: Book III: Waiting For Death — Chapter XXVII
paragraphs:
Let the high Muse chant loves Olympian:
We are but mortals, and must sing of man.

A distinguished philosopher I know, who can lend dignity even to ugly furniture by bringing it into the calm light of science, once showed me a small but revealing fact. A tall mirror, or a broad sheet of polished steel kept bright by a housemaid, has countless tiny scratches running in every direction. Set a burning candle before it, however, and suddenly those scratches seem to form beautiful concentric circles around that little sun. We can prove that the scratches run impartially every which way: the flattering pattern exists only because the candle lights up a particular selection of them. There is a parable here. The scratches are events; the candle is the self-importance of someone who is not present—Miss Vincy, for instance. Rosamond had her own private Providence. It had kindly made her more attractive than other girls, and now seemed to have arranged Fred’s illness and Mr. Wrench’s mistake so that she and Lydgate could be brought usefully close together. To go away to Stone Court or anywhere else, as her parents wished, would have frustrated these arrangements, especially when Mr. Lydgate himself considered the precaution unnecessary. So, while Miss Morgan and the children were sent to a farmhouse on the morning after Fred’s illness became clear, Rosamond refused to abandon her father and mother.

Her poor mother, indeed, would have moved any human heart. Mr. Vincy, devoted to his wife, was more frightened for her than for Fred. Without his insistence she would never have rested. All her brightness had faded. She no longer noticed the clothes she had always kept so fresh and cheerful; she resembled a sick bird, its eyes dull and feathers ruffled, scarcely registering the sights and sounds that usually interested her most. Fred’s delirium broke her heart: he seemed to be wandering somewhere she could not follow. After her first angry outburst against Mr. Wrench she became very quiet. Her one low appeal was to Lydgate. She would follow him from the room, lay a hand on his arm, and moan, “Save my boy.” Once she begged, “He’s always been good to me, Mr. Lydgate. He’s never spoken harshly to his mother”—as though Fred’s suffering were a charge she must defend him against. The deepest strands of her maternal memory had come alive. This young man, whose voice softened whenever he addressed her, was still the baby she had loved before his birth with a love she had never known before.

“I have every reason to hope, Mrs. Vincy,” Lydgate would tell her. “Come downstairs with me and we’ll discuss his food.” This brought her into the parlor with Rosamond and gave her a change, while he gently surprised her into drinking some tea or broth prepared for her. He and Rosamond were continually cooperating over such things. He nearly always saw her before entering the sickroom, and she asked his advice about helping her mother. She showed admirable composure and skill in acting on his suggestions. It was hardly surprising that the prospect of seeing Rosamond began to blend with his concern for the patient, especially once the crisis had passed and he felt confident that Fred would recover. While the outcome was still uncertain, he had recommended consulting Dr. Sprague, who would have preferred to stay out of the case for Wrench’s sake. After two consultations, though, Lydgate was left in charge, with every reason to give his closest attention. He visited the Vincys morning and evening. Gradually these visits grew cheerful: Fred was now merely weak, needing every possible indulgence and quite aware that he needed it. Mrs. Vincy began to feel that the illness, after all, had turned into a celebration of her motherly tenderness.

Both parents found a further cause for cheer when old Mr. Featherstone sent word through Lydgate that Fred must hurry up and recover: he, Peter Featherstone, could not do without the boy and sorely missed his visits. The old man was becoming confined to bed himself. Mrs. Vincy repeated these messages when Fred was well enough to listen. He turned his fine, shrunken face toward her; his thick fair hair had been cut off, and his eyes looked larger than before. He was longing for news of Mary, wondering how she felt about his illness. He said nothing. But lovers, with their rare understanding, can listen with their eyes, and his mother, in the fullness of her affection, not only guessed his wish but felt willing to make any sacrifice to grant it.
“If only I can see my boy strong again,” she said, foolish with love. “And who knows? Perhaps master of Stone Court! Then he can marry anyone he pleases.”
“Unless she won’t have me, Mother,” Fred answered. Illness had made him like a child, and the words brought tears.
“Here, darling, have a little jelly,” said Mrs. Vincy, privately unable to believe anyone could refuse him.

Whenever her husband was out, she stayed beside Fred. Rosamond consequently found herself alone much more often than usual. Lydgate naturally had no intention of lingering with her, yet their short, impersonal conversations seemed to be producing that peculiar intimacy which takes the form of shyness. They had to look at each other when they spoke, but somehow this ordinary necessity could not remain ordinary. Lydgate began to find the self-consciousness uncomfortable. One day his eyes darted down or anywhere else, like a puppet badly handled. This did not improve matters: next day Rosamond lowered hers, and when their eyes finally met, they were both more embarrassed than ever. Science offered no remedy, and since Lydgate had no wish to flirt, foolishness seemed to offer none either. He was therefore relieved when their neighbors stopped treating the house as a place of quarantine, and his chances of finding Rosamond alone became much fewer.

Yet once two people have shared that embarrassed awareness of each other’s feelings, its effects cannot simply be erased. Polite conversation about the weather begins to sound like an empty contrivance. Ease is difficult to recover without openly acknowledging a mutual attraction—which need not, of course, imply anything serious or profound. Rosamond and Lydgate gracefully found their way back to ease like this, and their conversations grew lively again. Visitors resumed coming and going, music returned to the drawing room, and Mr. Vincy’s extra hospitality as mayor was fully restored. Whenever possible, Lydgate sat beside Rosamond and lingered to hear her play, calling himself her captive while intending all along to remain free. The very absurdity of imagining that he could immediately afford a satisfactory married household seemed protection enough. Playing at being a little in love was pleasant and did not obstruct his more important work. After all, flirtation did not inevitably mean getting burned. Rosamond, meanwhile, had never enjoyed life so much. Someone worth capturing plainly admired her, and she drew no distinction between flirtation and love, whether in herself or anyone else. She seemed to be sailing on a favorable wind directly toward her chosen destination. Much of her attention went to a handsome house in Lowick Gate which she hoped would soon become vacant. Once married, she meant to find tactful ways of dropping all her father’s visitors whom she disliked, and she pictured various arrangements of furniture in that house’s drawing room.

She certainly thought a great deal about Lydgate too. He appeared almost faultless. If he could only read music, so that his rapt response to her playing had been a little less like an emotional elephant’s, and if he had appreciated the fine distinctions of her taste in clothes more accurately, she could hardly have named a failing. What a contrast to young Plymdale or Mr. Caius Larcher! Neither knew any French or could display impressive knowledge of anything except, perhaps, dyeing and the transport business—subjects they were naturally ashamed to bring up. They were Middlemarch gentlemen, proud of their silver-handled whips and satin neckcloths, awkward in company and timid in their jokes. Even Fred surpassed them, possessing at least a university man’s manner and accent. People always listened to Lydgate. He had the easy courtesy of someone conscious of his superiority, and the right clothes seemed to find him through some natural affinity, without his having to think about them. Rosamond felt proud when he entered a room. When he singled her out with a smile, she enjoyed the delicious knowledge that others must envy the attention paid to her. Had Lydgate known how much pride he stirred in her delicate breast, he might have been as pleased as any man, including one entirely ignorant of bodily humors or fibrous tissue. He thought it one of the prettiest feminine traits to worship a man’s distinction without knowing too precisely what it consisted of. But Rosamond was no helpless girl who accidentally gave herself away, her actions clumsily propelled by feeling instead of guided by cautious grace and propriety. Do you suppose her swift plans and private reflections about furniture and society ever showed in her conversation, even with her mother? Quite the reverse. Had she heard of another young woman caught thinking ahead so immodestly, she would have shown the most charming surprise and disapproval, and probably refused to believe it possible. Rosamond never displayed knowledge unsuitable for a young lady. She remained that blend of proper opinions, music, dancing, drawing, graceful correspondence, a private album of copied poetry, and flawless fair beauty that made a woman irresistible to the doomed man of her time. Please do not judge her unfairly. She harbored no wicked schemes and no mean or mercenary intentions. She scarcely thought about money except as a necessity that other people would always supply. She did not habitually invent lies. If her remarks gave no reliable indication of the facts, that was not their purpose: they belonged among her elegant accomplishments and were meant to please. Nature had used many arts in completing Mrs. Lemon’s favorite pupil, whom everyone but Fred agreed to be an exceptional mixture of beauty, intelligence, and sweetness.

Lydgate enjoyed her company more and more. All awkwardness had disappeared. Their eyes now exchanged a delightful influence, and their words carried that abundance of private meaning which can sound rather flat to a third person. Still, there were no private meetings or whispered exchanges that required anyone else to withdraw. They were flirting, in fact, and Lydgate remained confident that this was all they were doing. If a man could not be both in love and sensible, surely he could flirt and keep his judgment? The men of Middlemarch, apart from Mr. Farebrother, were terribly dull. Lydgate cared nothing for business politics or cards, so where else could he find relaxation? The Bulstrodes often invited him, but their daughters were scarcely out of the schoolroom. Mrs. Bulstrode’s innocent reconciliations of religion and worldliness—life’s emptiness and the attractions of cut glass, human righteousness as filthy rags and the merits of fine damask—did not sufficiently lighten her husband’s unvarying gravity. For all its faults, the Vincy household was more agreeable. And it contained Rosamond, as lovely to look at as a half-open pink rose, equipped with accomplishments for a man’s refined enjoyment.

His success with Miss Vincy, however, won him enemies outside medicine as well. One evening he arrived in the drawing room rather late and found several visitors there. The older people had gathered around the card table. Mr. Ned Plymdale, counted among Middlemarch’s desirable husbands though not its great intellects, was alone in conversation with Rosamond. He had brought the latest “Keepsake,” that splendid publication bound in watered silk which then represented modern progress. He felt particularly fortunate to be the first to examine it with her. He lingered over the engraved ladies and gentlemen, with their glossy copperplate cheeks and smiles, praising the comic verses as excellent and the sentimental stories as interesting. Rosamond received his attentions graciously. Ned was satisfied that he had chosen the finest possible offering of art and literature for a courtship—the very thing an agreeable girl would like. He also had reasons, more inward than apparent, for approving his own appearance. A casual observer might have thought his chin was retreating, as though being slowly absorbed back into his face. It certainly made it difficult to fit his satin neckcloths, for which a chin was then a useful support.
“I think the Honorable Mrs. S. resembles you,” Ned said. He held the book open at the enchanting portrait and gazed at it with a rather lovesick air.

“She has a very broad back. She seems to have posed to show it,” Rosamond replied. She meant no satire; she was thinking how red young Plymdale’s hands were and wondering why Lydgate had not arrived. Her fingers went on making tatted lace.
“I didn’t mean she was as lovely as you,” Ned said, daring to turn his eyes from the portrait to its rival.
“I suspect you’re a very practiced flatterer,” Rosamond answered, certain she would have to refuse this young man a second time.

Just then Lydgate arrived. Before he reached Rosamond’s corner, the book was shut. As he settled confidently on her other side, young Plymdale’s jaw dropped like a barometer forecasting unpleasant weather. Rosamond relished both Lydgate’s company and its effect on his rival. She enjoyed making men jealous.
“How late you are!” she said as they shook hands. “Mamma gave up expecting you a little while ago. How is Fred?”
“Much the same—improving, but slowly. I’d like him to go somewhere else, Stone Court, perhaps. Your mother seems to object.”
“Poor dear!” Rosamond said prettily. Then she turned to her other admirer. “You’ll find Fred terribly changed. Through all this illness we’ve looked on Mr. Lydgate as our guardian angel.”
Ned gave a nervous smile. Meanwhile Lydgate pulled the “Keepsake” toward him and opened it. A brief contemptuous laugh escaped him, and he lifted his chin as if marveling at human stupidity.
“What has provoked that irreverent laugh?” asked Rosamond, pleasantly noncommittal.

“I’m trying to decide which is sillier, the pictures or the writing,” Lydgate said with complete assurance. He flicked rapidly through the pages as though he could grasp the whole book at once, displaying his large white hands to excellent advantage, Rosamond thought. “Look at this bridegroom leaving the church. Have you ever seen such a sugary invention, as an Elizabethan might call it? Could even a haberdasher produce that smirk? Yet I’ll guarantee the story describes him as one of the country’s finest gentlemen.”
“You’re so harsh, you frighten me,” said Rosamond, keeping her amusement within proper limits. Unfortunately, young Plymdale had admired this very picture at length, and he rose to its defense.
“Well, plenty of famous people contribute to the ‘Keepsake,’” he said, sounding both offended and uncertain. “I’ve never heard anyone call it silly before.”

“Perhaps I ought to turn on you and call you a barbarian,” Rosamond told Lydgate with a smile. “I suspect you know nothing of Lady Blessington or L. E. L.” She enjoyed those writers herself, but was slow to commit herself to praise and quick to notice the smallest suggestion that Lydgate did not consider something the height of good taste.
“But Sir Walter Scott—surely Mr. Lydgate knows him,” young Plymdale put in, encouraged a little by this advantage.

“I don’t read literature these days,” said Lydgate, closing the book and pushing it aside. “I read so much as a boy that I imagine the supply will last a lifetime. I used to recite Scott’s poems from memory.”
“I’d like to know when you stopped reading,” Rosamond said. “Then I could be certain of knowing something you don’t.”
“Mr. Lydgate would probably say it wasn’t worth knowing,” Ned remarked, deliberately sharp.
“Quite the opposite,” Lydgate replied, apparently untouched, smiling at Rosamond with infuriating confidence. “Anything Miss Vincy could teach me would be worth learning for that reason alone.”
Young Plymdale soon moved away to watch the whist players. He considered Lydgate one of the most conceited and disagreeable men he had ever had the misfortune to encounter.
“How reckless of you!” Rosamond said, secretly delighted. “Didn’t you notice you’d offended him?”
“What—does the book belong to Mr. Plymdale? I’m sorry. That never occurred to me.”
“I’m beginning to believe what you told us when you first came: that you’re a bear who needs lessons from the birds.”
“There’s certainly one bird who may teach me anything she likes. Don’t I listen gladly enough?”

To Rosamond, she and Lydgate were practically engaged. She had long carried the idea that they would eventually be engaged; and, as we know, ideas tend to become solid realities when the necessary materials are available. Lydgate did have an opposing idea: he meant to remain unattached. But his was merely an absence, a shadow thrown by other intentions that could themselves diminish. Circumstances were almost certain to favor Rosamond’s idea. Hers actively shaped events and watched through alert blue eyes. His lay sightless and untroubled, like a jellyfish dissolving without knowing it.

At home that evening he inspected his small glass vessels to see how a process of soaking was progressing, with his scientific interest quite undisturbed. He wrote his daily notes as precisely as ever. The thoughts he found hard to leave were ideal constructions concerning something other than Rosamond’s virtues; primitive tissue was still the beautiful unknown he pursued. He was also beginning to enjoy the growing, half-concealed quarrel between himself and the other doctors. It would probably become more open once Bulstrode announced how the new hospital was to be managed. There were encouraging signs, too, that the impression Lydgate had made elsewhere might compensate for rejection by some of Peacock’s former patients. A few days later, he happened to catch up with Rosamond on the Lowick road. He dismounted and walked beside her until a passing herd had safely gone by. Then a mounted servant stopped him with a request to attend a household of some importance where Peacock had never practiced. It was the second such summons he had received. The servant belonged to Sir James Chettam; the house was Lowick Manor.
